The most common meaning of pregnant is: a female who has a developing baby growing inside her body. When a woman (or female animal) is pregnant, she is carrying a baby that will be born in the future.

"She is pregnant." → She is going to have a baby.
"The pregnant woman sat carefully in her chair."
"The vet confirmed that the dog was pregnant."

This is the standard, neutral word for this condition. It is used in medical settings, everyday conversation, and formal writing alike. It is neither rude nor overly technical — it is simply the correct, accepted word.

How Pregnant Is Someone?

Pregnancy in humans lasts about nine months, and you can describe how far along someone is by using weeks or months.

"She is six weeks pregnant."
"She is five months pregnant."

Informally, people also say heavily pregnant to describe someone in the final stage of pregnancy — when the baby bump is large and birth is approaching. You might also hear visibly pregnant or newly pregnant to describe different stages.

Can You Say "Very Pregnant"?

Technically, pregnancy is an all-or-nothing condition in biology — you either are pregnant or you are not. There is no degree to it, unlike, say, being tired (you can be a little tired or very tired). So strictly speaking, "very pregnant" is not precise.

However, in casual, informal speech, people do say things like "She's very pregnant now" to mean that she is obviously and visibly far along in her pregnancy. This is understood by everyone but is informal — not the kind of language you would use in a medical report.
The Figurative Meaning: Full of Hidden Significance

This is where the word becomes especially rich and interesting.

Pregnant has a second, figurative meaning that has nothing to do with babies. It means loaded with deep meaning, significance, tension, or potential — far more than what is directly visible or stated on the surface.

The conceptual link between the two meanings is beautiful: just as a pregnant woman carries something important inside her that is not yet fully visible to the world, a pregnant moment, silence, or phrase carries something important inside it — something unspoken, unstated, or not yet revealed, but powerfully felt.

The Most Famous Use: A Pregnant Pause / A Pregnant Silence

This is the single most common figurative use of the word, and it appears constantly in literature, film, and formal writing.

A pregnant pause (or pregnant silence) is a silence that is full of meaning, tension, or emotion. It is not an empty or awkward silence — it is a silence that says something without words. It suggests that something significant is being held back, or that both people in a conversation are acutely aware of something that is not being spoken aloud.

"After she asked him whether he had been lying, there was a pregnant pause before he finally answered."

In that example, the pause is not just a delay. It is heavy with tension. The reader understands that the man is thinking carefully, perhaps guiltily, perhaps nervously — and all of that meaning lives inside the silence itself. That is what makes it pregnant.

Pregnant With Something

You can also say that something is pregnant with a particular quality, meaning it is filled with or loaded with that quality to a degree that is not immediately spoken or shown.

"His words were pregnant with anger." → His words carried a great deal of suppressed anger beneath the surface, even if he did not raise his voice.

"The situation was pregnant with possibility." → The situation was full of potential — great things could develop from it.

"The moment was pregnant with danger." → The moment felt heavy with the threat of something harmful about to happen.

In all of these cases, the idea is the same: something important is being held inside, not yet fully released or expressed, but very much present and powerful.

A Pregnant Moment

Similarly, a pregnant moment refers to a single point in time that feels intensely significant, heavy with meaning, or charged with emotion — even if nothing dramatic is visibly happening at that instant.

"There was a pregnant moment when their eyes met across the room and everything unsaid between them hung in the air."

In the literal sense (carrying a baby), pregnant is completely standard — used equally in casual speech, formal documents, and medical contexts. There is nothing unusual about its register.

In the figurative sense (pregnant pause, pregnant with meaning), the word leans toward the literary and formal. It appears most naturally in novels, formal essays, screenplays, and careful journalism. In casual everyday conversation between friends, you would be unlikely to hear someone say "there was a pregnant silence" — though it is not wrong to say it.
The One Thread That Connects Everything

No matter how it is used — literal or figurative — the word pregnant always carries one underlying idea:

Something important is being held inside, not yet fully visible to the world, but full of life, meaning, or consequence.

A pregnant woman holds a future life inside her. A pregnant pause holds unspoken words and emotions inside it. A situation pregnant with danger holds a threat inside it that has not yet broken out. The word is always about hidden fullness — something inward, something not yet released, but deeply significant.

Meaning 1 (Literal): A female carrying a developing baby inside her body.
"She is eight months pregnant."

Meaning 2 (Figurative): Full of hidden meaning, significance, tension, or potential — more than is directly expressed.
"A pregnant pause." / "Pregnant with possibility." / "A pregnant moment."
